content.title: About
content.content: Mushrooms are the edible fruiting bodies of fungi belonging to various species of the Basidiomycota and Ascomycota families. They have a mild, slightly earthy flavor and a tender, sometimes crisp texture. Mushrooms can be eaten raw, sautéed, boiled, baked, and are used in soups, sauces, salads, and sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms are not plants; they belong to their own kingdom, Fungi.
There are over 10,000 edible mushroom species, but culinary use focuses on button, oyster, shiitake, and porcini varieties.
Mushrooms can produce vitamin D when exposed to ultraviolet light.
Some mushrooms, such as shiitake, contain compounds that boost immune function.
Mushrooms can be cultivated on substrates like sawdust, straw, or coffee grounds in controlled environments.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms provide niacin, riboflavin, pyridoxine, and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of fresh mushrooms contain about 22 kcal, making them an excellent choice for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Selenium and ergothioneine in mushrooms protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune‑supporting
items.content: Beta‑glucans found in mushrooms stimulate macrophage and natural killer cell activity.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in mushrooms aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to certain mushroom varieties.

items.title: Toxic wild species
items.content: Foraging for wild mushrooms without expert knowledge can lead to poisoning from toxic species.

items.title: Foodborne contamination
items.content: Improper storage or cooking can allow bacterial or mold growth.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Mushrooms contain purines, so people with gout should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mushrooms can be eaten raw in salads, sautéed, stewed, baked, or added to soups and sauces. Before cooking, they are usually brushed clean with a damp cloth and sliced. For a sandwich, mushrooms are often sautéed with onion and seasonings, then placed between bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh mushrooms in the refrigerator in a paper bag or container that allows airflow. Use them within 3–5 days. For longer storage, blanch them 2–3 minutes and freeze.
